rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Homeostasis holds temperature, glucose, pH and body water near a set point by negative feedback. Sweating and shivering manage heat. Insulin and glucagon manage glucose. The kidney and antidiuretic hormone manage water. Positive feedback is the exception, not the rule.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Homeostasis is the keeping of a steady internal state while the outside changes: temperature, blood glucose, pH, water and salts.
Negative feedback detects a change and starts a response that pushes the value back toward the set point. The response switches off as the set point is approached.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Negative feedback opposes the change. It is not a bad outcome.  ·  Insulin lowers blood glucose. Glucagon raises it.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Body temperature is maintained by shivering (heat production) and sweating (cooling).  ·  Glucose homeostasis involves insulin (lowers) and glucagon (raises) hormones.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: If body temperature rises, skin vessels widen and sweat increases heat loss. If it falls, vessels narrow and shivering produces heat.

rows.text: Homeostasis = stability through negative feedback loops.  ·  Set point = normal value that the system tries to maintain.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Differentiate between acute (rapid) and chronic (long-term) responses.  ·  Understand the roles of the hypothalamus (temperature, hunger, thirst), pituitary, and adrenal glands.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Negative feedback: deviation triggers response that reverses the change  ·  Positive feedback: amplification of a response (e.g., childbirth)  ·  Homeostatic variables: temperature, pH, glucose concentration, osmolarity  ·  Regulatory centers: hypothalamus, pituitary gland, endocrine glands

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Homeostasis relies on sensor organs detecting changes and control centers responding.  ·  Feedback loops are essential for maintaining stable internal environments.  ·  Multiple systems work together (e.g., nervous, endocrine, muscular) to achieve homeostasis.  ·  Steady internal state.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: How does the kidneys contribute to fluid and electrolyte homeostasis?  ·  Describe the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and its stress response.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: If blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin promotes uptake and storage. If glucose falls, glucagon promotes release from liver glycogen. The two hormones pull in opposite directions.  ·  The kidneys keep water and salts by varying how much is reabsorbed. Antidiuretic hormone saves water when the body is short of it.  ·  Positive feedback, as in the intensification of labour contractions, drives a change further. It is the exception. Homeostasis of temperature and glucose is negative feedback.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Negative feedback.  ·  Insulin and glucagon.  ·  ADH and the kidney save water.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Sweating cools. Shivering warms.  ·  The set point is a range, not a single frozen number.  ·  Osmoregulation prevents dehydration by adjusting water intake and kidney function.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Order in a sequence is part of the answer.  ·  Do not call a timberline a snowline.  ·  Thermoregulation maintains body temperature around 37°C (98.6°F).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.  ·  The kidneys regulate fluid balance and electrolyte concentrations.  ·  Sensors detect changes, control centers respond, effectors implement changes.
